name: The North Lands
overview: North of the Middle Lands across the Narrow Strait lies one great island of fjords, snowy highlands, an inland lake ringed by hills and a rich eastern vale. Its people, the Leren, speak a daughter of the old Ainic tongue and descend from the northern kingdoms that stood with Aen's realm; they sailed with Aenor in the First Age as partners, never as subjects, and their fleets have ruled the strait ever since. In the Second Age orc and goblin bands crossed from the Dark Lands and the small crowns of the interior built their hill-forts against them; when the Necromancer took Aenor the strait became the border of his Order, and Leren ships carried refugees north for twelve centuries while the dwarves of the High Mountains and the hill crowns of Heodwa swore the Hill Pact against his raiders. In the Fourth Age the crowns of Lerendor and Lerendor's North were joined by marriage in 4A 411, the Treaty of the Narrow Strait of 4A 512 bound the North to Aenor's defence, and the counting houses of Eekedor became the North's bank and its court of arbitration. In 4A 1748 the High Crown leads the Leren Compact and tolls every ship that passes Sonargur, still smarting from the toll quarrel of 4A 1716 in Parim, while the smaller crowns, a lake league, a hill council, a dwarf hold and the travelling dwarf goblins of the southern hills look to Sonargur or to Parim as it suits them. Years in the data are one continuous count from the victory of Aen on the proposed lengths of the ages (First Age 1,675 years, Second Age 2,133, Third Age 1,260): 1A 1 is year 1, 2A 1 is 1,676, 3A 1 is 3,809 and 4A 1 is 5,069, so that the campaign year 4A 1748 is 6,816; every entry also carries its date in the Age-and-year form, which is the form the prose uses.

ages.name: The Ship-Bond
ages.summary: The Leren kingdoms of the strait coast made alliance with Aen's Aenor, and around 1A 207 Leren and Aenoran ships charted the strait together and founded Sonargur at the best harbour of the Leren shore. The North sailed with Aenor as a partner and kept its own kings.

ages.name: Partners, Not Subjects
ages.summary: As Aenor declined the Leren crowns kept the strait for themselves, and when King Edran gathered the Grand Alliance against Volgan, the North sent its fleets and its levies on the understanding, which Edran accepted, that they came as partners rather than subjects.

ages.name: The Raiding Years
ages.summary: In the middle of the Second Age orc and goblin bands from the Dark Lands crossed the Northern Dark Strait and burned the coasts, and the small crowns of the interior built the hill-forts that still crown their valleys. Late in the age the envoy and commander Avarin of Lerendor's North tried to keep the northern alliance with Aenor alive while her own country faced the raids, and when the Necromancer took Aenor in 2A 2133 the help the North sent arrived too late.

ages.name: The Strait Border
ages.summary: For the whole Third Age the Narrow Strait was the border of the Necromancer's Order. Leren fleets carried refugees north and raided the occupied coast, the North stayed free, and in 3A 806 the dwarves of the High Mountains and the hill crowns of Heodwa swore the Hill Pact against his raiders.

ages.name: The High Crown and the Treaty
ages.summary: After the restoration the Leren crowns were united by marriage in 4A 411 and swore the Treaty of the Narrow Strait with Aenor in 4A 512. Eekedor's counting houses founded the Arbitration Court in 4A 906, the Leren Compact bound the counting houses to the High Crown, and the toll quarrel of 4A 1716 taught the court of Sonargur to doubt the treaty.

countries.name: Lerendor

founding.story: The strait kingdom of Lerendor and the western ice-crown of Lerendor's North had been rivals and kin for a thousand years when King Ostrik of the Sonarvik married Queen Runild of Lerendor's North in 4A 411 and the two crowns were set on one head. The Speakers' Hall of shipowners and landholders from both realms was summoned to approve the union's taxes, and the High Crown of Lerendor and Lerendor's North has been the strongest power of the North Lands since that wedding.

roots.story: The Leren speak a daughter of the old Ainic tongue and descend from the northern kingdoms of men that stood beside Aen's realm, and they have always been proud that they came to Aen as partners and never as subjects. Their history as sailors begins with a whale. The Narrow Strait is shallow and full of shoals, and the Leren tell that before any chart was drawn the strait-whale that winters in the Leren water was the only creature that knew the deep channel, and that the first Leren captains learned the strait by following it. When Leren and Aenoran ships charted the strait together under the Ship-Bond of 1A 207, a Sonarvik captain led the Aenoran hulls through the shoals behind a sounding whale, and the Sonarvik founded Sonargur at the river mouth where the whale turned. From the whale come the strait's law and the Leren temper: the Strait Litany forbids killing a whale inside the strait; the Ship-Blessing opens when the whale comes in Lumae; every Leren pilot must sail the channel once behind it; the strait belongs to those who know its water, which is why Sonargur takes its dues from every hull that passes; and the High Crown's two halves, the strait kingdom and the western ice-crown of Lerendor's North, joined by the wedding of 4A 411, are said to be the two flukes of one tail. A Leren court takes it badly when anyone, Parim least of all, forgets which partner showed the other the way, and the Toll of Parim was remembered at Sonargur as exactly that forgetting.

sign.device: The two flukes of a sounding whale rising from the sea, black on strait blue.
sign.origin: The flukes are the strait-whale's, sounding in the deep channel as the Sonarvik captain followed it through the shoals with the Aenoran hulls behind him under the Ship-Bond of 1A 207. Sonargur's first harbour-lord had the flukes carved on the Singing Quay, and when the two crowns were united in 4A 411 the heralds made the two flukes stand for the strait kingdom and Lerendor's North, one tail of one beast.
sign.meaning: We know the way through. It promises the ships that pay their dues a pilot and a guarded channel and reminds Parim that the Leren led the Aenoran fleets into the strait, not the other way round; since the Toll of Parim, Sonargur's sailors say the whale has turned its back.

dynasties.name: House Sonarvik of the strait
dynasties.notable: The strait kings who founded Sonargur with the Ship-Bond; a king takes a number and both crowns' titles. King Ferlin III reigns in 4A 1748.

dynasties.name: House Heskdal of Lerendor's North
dynasties.notable: The old western crown of the ice country, joined to the Sonarvik by Queen Runild's marriage in 4A 411; the lords of Lerendor's North still name their children from the Heskdal line.

events.name: The Northern Kingdoms Stand with Aen
events.summary: Northern kingdoms of Ainic-speaking men stand beside Aen in the last years of the War of Men as partners, not subjects; the Leren count their freedom from that alliance.

events.name: The Ship-Bond
events.summary: Leren and Aenoran ships charted the strait together and the Sonarvik kings founded Sonargur at the best harbour of the Leren shore.

events.name: The Pilot Behind the Whale
events.summary: Under the Ship-Bond a Sonarvik captain leads the Aenoran hulls through the shoals of the Narrow Strait behind a sounding strait-whale, and Sonargur is founded where the whale turned.

events.name: The Leren Crowns United
events.summary: King Ostrik of the Sonarvik married Queen Runild of Lerendor's North, and the two crowns became the High Crown of Lerendor and Lerendor's North.

events.name: The Treaty of the Narrow Strait
events.summary: The High Crown and Aenor swore mutual defence across the strait, the old alliance the North has kept for twelve centuries.

events.name: The Burning of Nuadoso
events.summary: Sea orcs of Belonton burned the shared seat of Keredor-Hellekton; the next year the High Crown's fleet burned the sea-orc harbour of Notle in return, and the Dark Shore has respected Leren sails since.

events.name: The Toll of Parim
events.summary: Lerendor's envoys were humiliated before the Aenoran court over a disputed toll on Leren ships in Aenoran harbours, and the court of Sonargur began to ask what the treaty was worth.

rivalries.nature: The gateway principality that leans to Parim and holds the strait's southern cape.
The marcher state that balances Sonargur against Parim.

countries.capitalReason: Sonargur stands under Sonargur Point at the mouth of the Leren River, the best natural harbour of the Narrow Strait, where the strait dues can be taken from every ship that passes and the river brings the interior's goods to the sea.
countries.today: King Ferlin III rules some one and a fifth million people of the Leren shore, the river valley, Lerendor's North, the Low-ness Islands and Ferlinon's pine hills. The strait dues make the crown rich, the fleets guard the strait, the dwarves' bombards ride on the royal ships, and the court has not forgiven Parim for the toll of 4A 1716.

divergence.what: The High Crown honours the Treaty of the Narrow Strait when the last war comes.
divergence.consequence: Lerendor fights for Aenor and can bar the strait to its enemies, and the North keeps the old alliance.

divergence.what: The High Crown turns the war into Leren mastery of the strait.
divergence.consequence: Lerendor wars on R'en and claims the strait's southern shore, and the North becomes the strait's master rather than its keeper.

divergence.what: The court withdraws from the treaty before any war begins.
divergence.consequence: The North stands apart from the first day, and Aenor's northern flank is open.

countries.name: Eekedor

founding.story: The grain of the Eekedor Vale had always gone out through the blue inlet at Viktara, and the merchant families who bought it lent so much to the island's crowns that in 4A 620 they formed a council of counting houses to keep their books together and their debtors honest. The council has ruled the vale since, and in 4A 906 it founded the Arbitration Court where the North's crowns settle their feuds for a fee.

roots.story: The Eekedor Vale has always been the North's granary, and its people have always preferred to weigh a danger rather than fight it. In the Raiding Years, when orc and goblin bands crossed from the Dark Lands and the crowns of the interior raised hill-forts, a raider host came down the vale to Viktara in 2A 1205, and the grain-families met its chief at the harbour with the great steelyard on which they weighed the barges' grain. They hung his own sword from the hook and weighed it against grain, then against silver, then against what a siege would cost him in his men's lives, and told him the price of each; the host took the silver and left, and three of its captains stayed behind to guard the vale for wages. The vale has lived by the steelyard since. From it come the council's laws and its court: everything has a weight, and a quarrel is settled when both sides agree what it weighs; the counting houses lend to every crown, because a debtor weighs more than an enemy; the Arbitration Court founded in 4A 906 is the steelyard made into a bench, and the North's crowns pay to have their feuds weighed there; and the vale has never raised a great host of its own, because it has always found it cheaper to buy one. The old steelyard still hangs above the council's table at Viktara, and the Speakers say no grain has ever been weighed on it short.

sign.device: A black steelyard balance with its hanging weight, on gold.
sign.origin: The steelyard is the grain-weigher of Viktara's harbour, on which the grain-families weighed the raider chief's sword against grain, silver and blood in 2A 1205, and which has hung above the council's table since the counting houses formed their council in 4A 620. The Arbitration Court opens every judgement by hanging a weight on it, and the vale's bills of exchange bear its mark, so that a Viktara bill is honoured from Sonargur to Parim.
sign.meaning: Everything can be weighed. It promises every crown a fair judgement for a fair fee and every debtor an honest account; to its enemies it says that the vale will price their war before they start it, and to Dolpar's lake-court it is the scale of the North's first bench.

dynasties.name: The Speakers of the counting houses
dynasties.notable: The council of counting houses chooses a Speaker for five years; the Perhkov house of the salt-pans of Oirt has given the most Speakers.

events.name: The Weighing of the Sword
events.summary: The grain-families of Viktara weigh a raider chief's sword on the harbour steelyard against grain, silver and a siege's cost in lives; the host takes the silver and three of its captains stay as the vale's guards.

events.name: The Council of Counting Houses
events.summary: The merchant families of Viktara formed the council that has ruled the vale since.

events.name: The Arbitration Court
events.summary: The council founded the Arbitration Court, and the small crowns of the North began to settle their feuds there.

events.name: The Leren Compact
events.summary: Eekedor and the High Crown swore the Leren Compact, binding the North's grain and money to its fleets; the smaller crowns may join it, and some have.

events.name: The Marriage of the Coast Crowns
events.summary: The Arbitration Court settled the marriage that joined Keredor and Hellekton, the most famous judgement in its history.

rivalries.nature: The lake league's court, set up in 4A 1580 as a rival to Eekedor's arbitration.

countries.capitalReason: Viktara stands on the blue inlet of the vale where the grain barges come down to the sea, the one harbour of the island's rich east, and the counting houses built beside the granaries they lent against.
countries.today: About six hundred thousand people live in the Eekedor Vale with Oirt, Pertawn and Filit under the council of counting houses. Eekedor is the island's grain and money, keeps the Compact with the High Crown and holds its court open to any crown that pays.

divergence.what: The counting houses leave the Leren Compact over the strait dues.
divergence.consequence: Lerendor loses its bank, and the High Crown's fleets must be paid from the dues alone.

divergence.what: The Arbitration Court is asked to judge the toll quarrel between Sonargur and Parim.
divergence.consequence: The quarrel of 4A 1716 may end in a judgement rather than a war, and the court's name rises across Aoaz.

countries.name: R'en

founding.story: The strait cape at the Narrow Strait's narrowest point was a watch-post of the strait kings until 1A 1240, when its keeper, Torik of the Farnur, refused to pay the Sonarvik for the forts he had built and declared himself prince of the cape. He made his living on the Aenoran ships that passed under his walls, and his heirs have lived between two masters ever since, the strait kings across the water and the southern crown below the cape.

roots.story: The strait cape at the Narrow Strait's narrowest point has always belonged to whoever could sit on it, and its people have always taken a share of whatever passed. Before the strait kings built forts there, fisher-clans lived on the cape's rocks and took toll of every boat that crossed in the old way of the cape: a boat that passed under the rocks gave up one fish, and the clans called themselves cormorants, after the birds that sit on the same rocks between the two seas. When the cape became a watch-post of the strait kings its keepers kept the custom, and in 1A 1240 its keeper, Torik of the Farnur, whom the strait called the Cormorant, refused to pay the Sonarvik for the forts he had built and declared himself prince of the cape, living on the Aenoran ships that passed under his walls. From the cormorant come the principality's habits: a prince who serves two masters and is owned by neither; a toll on everything that passes, light enough to be paid rather than fought; a court that faces both seas, marrying into Parim and trading with Sonargur; and a stubbornness proved under the Order, when the princes held Farnardur as the North's southern gate for twelve centuries and twice beat off its hosts at the forts. The strait says a cormorant always keeps one eye on each sea, and the princes of R'en have never taken it as an insult.

sign.device: A black cormorant perched on a grey rock with a silver fish in its beak, on white.
sign.origin: The cormorant was Torik's own byname, from the cape-clans' custom of taking one fish from every boat that passed under the rocks, and he flew a painted cormorant over the forts of Farnardur when he refused the strait kings their payment in 1A 1240. The princes have kept it since, and every ship that pays the cape's toll is given a wooden token cut with the cormorant, so that it will not be asked again before the next tide.
sign.meaning: One fish from every boat, and no master. It promises passing ships a light toll and a safe passage and tells both Sonargur and Parim that the cape is the prince's; a cormorant with an empty beak on the forts would mean the strait was shut.

dynasties.name: The Farnur princes of the cape
dynasties.notable: Descended from Torik, the keeper who made himself prince; the princes marry into Aenoran houses more often than Leren ones.

events.name: The Cormorant Clans
events.summary: Fisher-clans on the rocks of the strait cape take one fish from every boat that passes beneath them and call themselves cormorants; the cape's toll is older than its forts.

events.name: The Prince of the Cape
events.summary: Torik of the Farnur refused to pay the strait kings for his forts and made himself prince of the cape.

events.name: The Strait Under the Order
events.summary: The princes held Farnardur as the North's southern gate against the Necromancer's Order for the whole occupation, and twice beat off its hosts at the forts.

events.name: The Aenoran Marriage
events.summary: A prince of R'en married a daughter of an Aenoran house close to the crown, and since then the cape has leaned openly to Parim.

rivalries.nature: The strait kings, who claim the cape and need its forts.

countries.capitalReason: Farnardur stands at the strait's narrowest point on the southern cape, where the forts command every ship that passes and the Sea of R'en behind gives a sheltered harbour.
countries.today: About three hundred thousand people live on the strait cape and around the Sea of R'en under a prince with two masters. R'en lives on Aenoran trade, leans to Parim, and knows that Lerendor's mastery of the strait would begin at its forts.

divergence.what: The prince bars the strait to Leren ships in Aenor's name.
divergence.consequence: Lerendor must take the cape or give up the strait, and the North's quarrel with Parim becomes a war on the cape.

divergence.what: The prince joins the Leren Compact.
divergence.consequence: The strait is wholly Leren, and Aenor loses its friend on the northern shore.

countries.name: Molot

founding.story: In the Raiding Years the northern march of the island took the worst of the raiders from the Dark Lands, and in 2A 1240 the strait kings gave its defence to Helmund of the Ostvar, who built a fortress line behind the marsh and was named margrave. The margraves kept the march long after the raids ended and learned to balance the High Crown against Parim, so that neither would ever think it needed to take the march for itself.

roots.story: The northern march of the island is a country of marsh and hill facing the Dark Shore, and the margraves were made by the Raiding Years. When orc and goblin bands began crossing from the Dark Lands in the Second Age they came through the marsh, which only its own folk could cross, along paths marked with stakes. In 2A 1240 the strait kings gave the march's defence to Helmund of the Ostvar, and the march tells his story as a single night: when a raider host came into the marsh, Helmund's men waded out in the dark and moved the path-stakes, and by dawn the host had walked into the deep water and drowned. The fortress line he built behind the marsh made him margrave. From the moved stakes come the march's customs and its politics: every marsh-path is staked anew each spring by the margrave's men alone, and a stranger who moves a stake is drowned; the margraves show the true path only to friends and change it when friends change; and they learned to stake the march's way between the High Crown and Parim in the same manner, leaning towards Aenor whenever Sonargur leans away, so that neither would ever think it needed to take the march for itself. The house of Ostvar also claims kin in the lords of Fotan across the strait, who bear the same name and neither confirm nor deny it.

sign.device: A single white path-stake standing crooked in black marsh water, on dark green.
sign.origin: The stake is one of those Helmund's men moved on the night the raider host drowned in the marsh in 2A 1240. The margraves keep it in the hall of Altovian, and the march's banner has shown it crooked ever since, because a stake that stands straight shows the true path; every spring the margrave drives the first new stake of the marsh-paths himself.
sign.meaning: The way through is ours to show. It promises friends a safe path and enemies the deep water, and tells Sonargur and Parim that the margrave decides which of them is shown the way this year.

dynasties.name: The Ostvar margraves of Altovian
dynasties.notable: Descended from Helmund, the first margrave; the margravate passes to the eldest son or daughter who has commanded a fort of the line.

events.name: The March Given
events.summary: Helmund of the Ostvar was named margrave and built the fortress line of the northern march.

events.name: The Night of the Moved Stakes
events.summary: Helmund of the Ostvar's men wade into the marsh by night and move the path-stakes, and a raider host out of the Dark Lands walks into the deep water and drowns before dawn.

events.name: The Harbour of Knorvik
events.summary: The margraves took the ship-bay of Knorvik from a coast crown that sold its harbour to whoever paid, and Molot has had its own harbour since.

events.name: The Margrave's Balance
events.summary: After the toll quarrel the margrave sent an envoy to Parim within the year, and Molot has leaned to Aenor whenever Sonargur leans away.

rivalries.nature: The High Crown, whose reach the margraves balance with Parim's friendship.

countries.capitalReason: Altovian is the margrave's fortress-town behind the marsh line, where the fortress line meets the road from Knorvik to the interior, built for defence rather than trade.
countries.today: About two hundred thousand people live in the northern march with the harbour of Knorvik under the margrave, whose forts are manned and whose envoys are in Parim. Molot leans to Aenor, which in the North is a way of not leaning to Sonargur.

divergence.what: The margrave declares for Aenor when the High Crown withdraws from the treaty.
divergence.consequence: The North is divided in the last war, and Lerendor must watch its march as well as the strait.

divergence.what: The margrave swears to the High Crown.
divergence.consequence: The North stands united behind Sonargur, and Parim loses its last friend on the island's west.

countries.name: Keredor-Hellekton

founding.story: The coast crowns of Keredor and Hellekton had fought over the pass of Belg for three generations when in 4A 1344 the Arbitration Court of Eekedor ruled that Queen Vigda of Keredor should marry King Helmund of Hellekton and that their children should hold both crowns and the pass between them. The two courts moved to the shared inlet of Nuadoso, and the double crown has been the North's best example of its custom of crown-sharing marriages.

roots.story: The coast crowns of Keredor and Hellekton are two halves of an old quarrel over one pass. The pass of Belg is the only road from the north coast's two harbours into the interior, and the two crowns, both grown in the Raiding Years from Leren coast-holds that had walled their harbours against the sea-orcs of the Dark Shore, fought over it for three generations, each crowning its kings in its own old hall and each refusing to let the other's king ride through the pass. The custom of the Leren North that neighbouring crowns may join by a marriage that sets both crowns on the heirs gave the Arbitration Court of Eekedor its most famous case, and in 4A 1344 it ruled that Queen Vigda of Keredor should marry King Helmund of Hellekton and that their children should hold both crowns and the pass between them. The smiths of the new shared seat at Nuadoso melted part of each old crown and forged one double crown of two circlets, Keredor's silver and Hellekton's gold, and because neither crown could be set above the other, the heir is crowned twice, once with each circlet uppermost, riding by night between the two old halls. From the double crown come the realm's habits: two of everything, two halls, two councils, two coronations; an inherited fear of being shared out again; and a debt to Sonargur, whose fleet burned the sea-orc harbour of Notle the year after the sea-orcs burned Nuadoso in 4A 1531, which brought the double crown into the Leren Compact.

sign.device: A double crown of two stacked circlets, the lower silver and the upper gold, on sea grey.
sign.origin: The double crown was forged at Nuadoso after the Marriage of the Coast Crowns in 4A 1344 from the metal of both old crowns, Keredor's silver and Hellekton's gold. Because neither crown may stand above the other, the heir is crowned with it twice, once with each circlet uppermost, and the banner is turned the same way: Keredor's hall flies it with the silver above, Hellekton's with the gold above, and the shared seat flies both side by side.
sign.meaning: Two crowns, one realm, and neither above the other. It promises each coast that it will never be second and warns any neighbour that the pass of Belg is held by both crowns at once; if the banners ever stopped being turned, the North would know that the double crown had split.

dynasties.name: The house of Vigda and Helmund
dynasties.notable: The joint line of the two coast crowns; each heir is crowned twice, once in each crown's old hall, before taking the seat at Nuadoso.

events.name: The Marriage of the Coast Crowns
events.summary: The Arbitration Court married Queen Vigda of Keredor to King Helmund of Hellekton and joined the crowns and the pass of Belg.

events.name: The Double Crown Forged
events.summary: The smiths of Nuadoso forge one double crown from the metal of the two old crowns, Keredor's silver below and Hellekton's gold above, and the first heir is crowned with each circlet uppermost in turn.

events.name: The Burning of Nuadoso
events.summary: Sea orcs of Belonton burned the shared seat; the High Crown's fleet burned Notle in return the next year, and the double crown joined the Leren Compact in gratitude.

events.name: The Two Coronations
events.summary: A quarrel over which old hall should crown the heir first was settled by crowning him in both on the same day, riding between them by night.

countries.capitalReason: Nuadoso is the shared inlet between the two coast crowns, chosen because it belonged to neither and could be reached by both courts by sea in a day.
countries.today: About a quarter of a million people live on the two coast crowns and the pass of Belg under the double crown, a member of the Leren Compact since the burning of its seat. Its court still crowns every heir twice.

divergence.what: A disputed succession splits the double crown back into two.
divergence.consequence: The pass of Belg is fought over again, and the North's custom of crown-sharing loses its proudest example.

divergence.what: The double crown takes ship against the Dark Shore to avenge Nuadoso.
divergence.consequence: The North's quarrel with Belonton reopens, and the Dark Sea Accord loses a partner's attention when it most needs it.

countries.name: Tolvael

founding.story: The long vale of Tolvael, with its fjord at Goran and its iron hill at Kerhil, was the richest valley of the island's interior, and in 1A 1360 its landholders crowned Brann of the Agtos king in the vale town of Agtosai so that the vale would not be shared out among the coast crowns. Tolvael has been the first and proudest of the North's free crowns ever since.

roots.story: The long vale of Tolvael is the richest valley of the island's interior, and for most of its history the coast crowns have wanted to split it like a log. Its people are timber-folk, felling the great pines of the vale's slopes and boiling their tar, and their oldest craft secret is the heartwood of the old pines of the iron hill Kerhil, which grows so hard that a common axe breaks on it. In 1A 1360, when the coast crowns of the island proposed to share the vale out among themselves, the vale's landholders met at Agtosai, and the vale's story is that each envoy of the coast crowns was handed an axe and asked to split a Kerhil pine log that lay before the hall; every axe broke, and the landholders crowned Brann of the Agtos king seated on the unsplit log and sent the envoys home without their axe-heads. From the log come Tolvael's customs: every king is crowned seated on a Kerhil log; the vale is never divided between heirs, so a king's younger sons get timber rights and no land; the free crowns of the North owe Tolvael their pride, as the first crown that refused to be shared; and the vale cooperates gladly with the High Crown when it is asked and not at all when it is told, for the axe-heads of the coast crowns are still nailed above the hall door at Agtosai.

sign.device: An unsplit black pine log lying across the field with a broken axe-head beside it, on dark green.
sign.origin: The log is the Kerhil pine on which the landholders crowned Brann of the Agtos in 1A 1360, after every axe the coast crowns' envoys brought had broken on it. The axe-heads are nailed above the hall door at Agtosai, and a new king's first act is to strike the log of his crowning with one of them, so that the vale can hear it fail to split.
sign.meaning: The vale will not be split. It promises Tolvael's people one king and one undivided land and tells every coast crown and the High Crown that Tolvael gives when it is asked; an axe that split the log would mean the end of the vale as a free crown.

dynasties.name: The Agtos kings of the vale
dynasties.notable: Descended from Brann, the first king; the landholders' council confirms each heir, and the kings have sent their younger sons to the strait fleets for generations.

events.name: The Crowning in the Vale
events.summary: The landholders of the long vale crowned Brann of the Agtos at Agtosai.

events.name: The Envoys' Axes
events.summary: The envoys of the coast crowns are asked to split a Kerhil pine log before the hall at Agtosai, and every axe breaks; the landholders crown Brann of the Agtos on the unsplit log and keep the axe-heads.

events.name: The Hill-Forts
events.summary: In the Raiding Years Tolvael built the hill-forts that crown the vale and beat off three raider hosts from the Dark Lands.

events.name: The Tar Trade
events.summary: Tolvael's timber and pine tar became the strait fleets' supply, and the vale has grown rich on every ship the North has built since.

countries.capitalReason: Agtosai lies in the middle of the long vale where the road from Goran's fjord meets the road to the iron hill, the vale's market and its natural seat.
countries.today: About four hundred thousand people live in the long vale with Goran's fjord and the iron hill Kerhil, the most populous of the small crowns. Tolvael is proud, rich in timber and tar, and a willing partner of the High Crown as long as it is asked rather than told.

divergence.what: Tolvael joins the Leren Compact as the first of the small crowns.
divergence.consequence: The Compact grows toward hegemony, and the smaller crowns follow the vale.

divergence.what: Tolvael leads the small crowns in a league of their own against Sonargur's reach.
divergence.consequence: The North divides between the High Crown and the free crowns, and the strait fleets lose their timber.

countries.name: Tolhon

founding.story: The west coast of the island faces the small sea of the Onp, and its isles and toll-bridge town at Sirtum were held by a dozen lords until in 4A 260 Ulvek of the Ishor took the harbour of Migur and the bridge and made himself prince of the coast and the isles. Tolhon has been an island principality since, living by its toll-bridge, its fisheries and its distance from everyone else's quarrels.

roots.story: The west coast of the island faces the small sea of the Onp, and its people have lived by herring for as long as there have been boats on it. Long before the princes, the Onp fishers kept the Herring Peace: no feud was carried on, no boat burned and no toll taken while the herring were running, because the fishers believed that the herring would leave a sea where men fought over them. The dozen lords who held the coast's isles and the toll-bridge of Sirtum kept the peace badly, and when Ulvek of the Ishor took the harbour of Migur and the bridge in 4A 260 and made himself prince of the coast, he did it in the season after the run, and swore at the bridge to keep the Herring Peace as the coast's first law. The princes' authority has rested on the herring since. When the herring left the Onp for a whole generation, it was the prince who forbade the summer nets until they came back in 4A 1610, and the fishers have kept the ban ever since. From the herring come the principality's customs: no war is begun in the run; the toll-bridge of Sirtum, rebuilt in stone by dwarf masons of the High Mountains, pays the prince so that the fishers need not; the prince stays out of the strait's quarrels, because a sea at war is a sea without herring; and the coast measures its prince by the size of the catch. The packmen of Mustnom, barred from the bridge after the Sirtum Brawl, say Tolhon's princes care more for fish than for men, and the coast agrees.

sign.device: A silver herring leaping above a single grey stone bridge-arch, on Onp blue.
sign.origin: The herring and the arch are the Herring Peace and the bridge of Sirtum, where Ulvek of the Ishor swore in 4A 260 to keep the peace of the run as the coast's first law. When the herring came back in 4A 1610 after a generation away, the prince's ban on summer nets was proclaimed at the bridge under a banner showing the silver herring over the arch, and Tolhon has flown it since.
sign.meaning: Peace in the run, toll at the bridge. It promises the fishers a prince who keeps the herring's peace before any other and tells the strait's quarrelling crowns that Tolhon will not bring their war into its sea.

dynasties.name: The Ishor princes of Migur
dynasties.notable: Descended from Ulvek, the first prince; the principality passes to the eldest child, and the princes take their name from the fish isle where their line began.

events.name: The Herring Peace
events.summary: The fishers of the Onp keep the Herring Peace: no feud, no burning and no toll while the herring run, lest the herring leave a sea where men fight over them.

events.name: The Prince of the Onp Coast
events.summary: Ulvek of the Ishor took Migur and the toll-bridge of Sirtum and founded the principality.

events.name: The Sirtum Bridge Rebuilt
events.summary: The princes rebuilt the river-bridge of Sirtum in stone with dwarf masons from the High Mountains, and its tolls have paid for the principality since.

events.name: The Gaci Herring
events.summary: The herring left the Onp for a whole generation and returned only when the prince forbade the summer nets; Tolhon's fishers still keep the ban.

countries.capitalReason: Migur is the one harbour of the west coast sheltered from both the Onp and Londolo, close to the toll-bridge of Sirtum and the isles of Gaci and Ishor.
countries.today: About two hundred thousand people live on the west coast with Ashorn, Sirtum and the isles under their prince. Tolhon takes its tolls, keeps its herring ban and stays out of the strait's quarrels.

divergence.what: The prince joins the Leren Compact.
divergence.consequence: The High Crown's reach extends to the Onp, and the west coast's toll-bridge serves Sonargur.

divergence.what: Tolhon's ships watch Londolo for landings in the last war.
divergence.consequence: The North has warning of anything that comes from the west, and the principality's quiet ends.

countries.name: Heodwa Lands

founding.story: The three hill crowns of the island's centre, Heodwa, Nuatax and Agniy, had fought each other for centuries until the Necromancer's raiders came up the valleys in the Third Age. In 3A 806 their kings met the dwarves of the High Mountains at Pand and swore the Hill Pact, under which the dwarves would come down to any hill crown that was attacked; the three kings formed one hill council to keep the pact, and the council has ruled the hills since.

roots.story: The three hill crowns of the island's centre, Heodwa, Nuatax and Agniy, fought each other for so long that each claims to have raised the first hill-fort, and the hills are covered with the forts of their wars. Their kings had one custom in common, older than their quarrels: a great horn blown from a hill-top called every hill-clan to arms, and a crown that answered no horn but its own was a crown alone. When the Necromancer's raiders came up the valleys in the Third Age the three kings learned that they were alone in exactly that sense, and in 3A 806 they met the dwarves of the High Mountains at Pand. The dwarves would not swear on a crown, and the kings would not swear on a dwarf-forge; they swore instead on one great horn, which the dwarves bound with three rings of gold, one for each crown, so that whoever blew it at Pand would call down the dwarves and all three hill crowns at once. That is the Hill Pact, and it was first tested in 3A 1022, when the horn was blown from Pand and the dwarves came down the valley of Nuatax and broke the Order's raiders. From the horn comes the hill council: one horn, so one council; three rings, so three voices; a war on one crown is a war on all and on the White Hall; and no hill crown may blow the horn for its own quarrel, the oldest rule of the council and the one most often argued. When the Mulchy Lands came under the council's protection in 4A 1460, their voice was given a cord on the horn, not a ring.

sign.device: A great black horn banded with three gold rings, on hill green.
sign.origin: The horn of Pand is the one on which the three hill kings and the dwarves of the High Mountains swore the Hill Pact in 3A 806, bound by the dwarves with three gold rings for the three crowns. It was blown from Pand in 3A 1022 to call the dwarves down the valley of Nuatax, it hangs in the council hall at Pand, and the hill council has flown it since the pact.
sign.meaning: Blow, and the hills and the mountain answer. It promises every hill crown that it is never alone and warns every crown of the North that a war on Heodwa calls down Hrakbrund; the council's own fear is the day someone blows it for the wrong war.

dynasties.name: The hill council of the three crowns
dynasties.notable: The three hill crowns keep their own kings, who sit together in the council at Pand and choose one of themselves to speak for the hills each year.

events.name: The Hill Pact
events.summary: The three hill crowns and the dwarves of the High Mountains swore the Hill Pact against the Necromancer's raiders, and the hill council was born of it.

events.name: The Horn of Pand Bound
events.summary: The dwarves of the High Mountains bind a great horn with three gold rings, one for each hill crown, and the Hill Pact is sworn on it at Pand; whoever blows it calls down the dwarves and all three crowns.

events.name: The Dwarves Come Down
events.summary: Raiders of the Order came up the valley of Nuatax, and for the first time the dwarves came down from the High Mountains under the pact and broke them.

events.name: The Mulchy Lands Taken In
events.summary: The council took the peat-country of the Mulchy Lands under its protection, and its folk sent a voice to the council at Pand.

countries.capitalReason: Pand is the council town where the roads of the three hill crowns meet below the High Mountains, the place where the kings first met the dwarves and swore the pact.
countries.today: About a quarter of a million people live in the central hills with Nuatax, Agniy and the Mulchy Lands under the hill council. The Hill Pact still binds the dwarves to the hills, and every crown of the North knows that a war on Heodwa is a war on Hrakbrund.

divergence.what: The hill council calls on the Hill Pact in the last war.
divergence.consequence: The dwarves of Hrakbrund come down from their mountains, and the North gains the only dwarf host that has left its hold in an age.

divergence.what: The three hill crowns quarrel and the council breaks.
divergence.consequence: The Hill Pact lapses, and the dwarves close their High Gate to the hills.

countries.name: Hrakbrund

founding.story: The dwarves of the High Mountains count their years from their own first delving and keep that count to themselves; men date the hold from 1A 110, when the Leren first traded at its High Gate for iron and gold. Their deep hall under the snows, Ilmahrim, the white hall, is ruled by the lord of the eldest delving line, and men are received only at the gate.

roots.story: The dwarves of the High Mountains were the northern arm of the Stone Road, the dwarves' realm of deep roads under the sea, and their road ran under the Narrow Strait to the holds of the south. When the Damned Spirits came into the roads in Volgan's war, Hrakbrund sealed the road under the strait with the names of its last delvers cut into the door, and it has had no Deep King since. Its lords learned something the other holds did not: cut off from their kin, they could live only by the men of the island, and the White Hall became the hold that trades the most with men. It learned too that a hold can wait in its mountain while the world burns, and that it should not. When the Necromancer's raiders came up the hill valleys in the Third Age, the hill kings of Heodwa came to Pand to ask for help, and in the winter after the Hill Pact of 3A 806 the lord of the White Hall had a stair cut from the High Gate down the mountain to the valley floor, wide enough for a column, so that the dwarves could come down in a day; it was used in 3A 1022, when the dwarves came down the valley of Nuatax and broke the Order's raiders. From the Coming-Down Stair come the hold's ways: the dwarves of the White Hall hold that a hold which never comes down is only a tomb; every young dwarf of the hold walks down the stair once to see the hill crowns; the bombards sold to Sonargur since 4A 1612 go down the stair; and the hold's old grudge against elves cools any court that seats an elven envoy.

sign.device: A white stair descending from the upper right to the lower left, on black.
sign.origin: The stair is the Coming-Down Stair, cut from the High Gate down the mountain in the winter after the Hill Pact of 3A 806 so that the dwarves could reach the hill crowns in a day. The Ilmord lords have borne it since the dwarves first came down it in 3A 1022 to break the Order's raiders in the valley of Nuatax, and its lowest step is the boundary stone of the Hill Pact.
sign.meaning: The mountain comes down for its friends. It promises the hill crowns the dwarves within a day and the High Crown its bombards; to an enemy of Heodwa it says the stair is wide enough for a column, and to the other holds it says that Hrakbrund chose men over the moot.

dynasties.name: The Ilmord lords of the White Hall
dynasties.notable: The line that rules from the white hall; the present lord, Hradin Ilmord, keeps the Hill Pact and receives no elf at his gate.

events.name: The High Gate Opened
events.summary: The dwarves of the High Mountains opened their High Gate to Leren traders.

events.name: The Northern Sea-Door Sealed
events.summary: The hold seals the road that ran under the strait to the other holds, cutting the names of its last delvers into the door, and has had no Deep King since.

events.name: The Hill Pact
events.summary: The hold swore the Hill Pact with the three hill crowns of Heodwa against the Necromancer's raiders.

events.name: The Coming-Down Stair Cut
events.summary: In the winter after the Hill Pact the lord of the White Hall has a stair cut from the High Gate down the mountain to the valley floor, wide enough for a column of dwarves to come down in a day.

events.name: The Dwarves Come Down
events.summary: Under the pact the dwarves came down into the valley of Nuatax and broke the Order's raiders.

events.name: The Bombards of Sonargur
events.summary: The hold sold its first bombards to the High Crown, and the royal ships of the strait have carried them since.

countries.capitalReason: Ilmahrim, the white hall, lies deep under the snows of the High Mountains where the richest veins of iron and gold run; the High Gate below it is where men trade, because men go no further.
countries.today: About fifty thousand dwarves hold the High Mountains and the Loso heights, sell iron, gold and bombards at the High Gate and keep the Hill Pact with Heodwa. Sonargur's fleets need their bombards, and an elven envoy at Sonargur's court cools the hold at once.

divergence.what: The hold arms Sonargur's mastery of the strait with its best bombards.
divergence.consequence: The High Crown's fleets can break any fort on the strait, and the hold's favour becomes the price of the North.

divergence.what: An elven envoy at Sonargur or a broken contract closes the High Gate.
divergence.consequence: The North's fleets go without new bombards, and the High Crown learns how much it leaned on the dwarves.

countries.name: Mina

founding.story: The ore hills of Etonia had been dug for iron since the Second Age by miners who owed their lord a share of every cartload, and in 4A 640 the miners' lord, Stenolf of the Korn, opened the great galleries the North calls the Delvings and was crowned king of the ore hills at Gilvian. Mina has been the North's mining crown since, with its sister crown of Mine Din joined to it by marriage.

roots.story: The ore hills of Etonia were dug for iron by Leren miners from the Second Age, who owed their lord a share of every cartload and lived in fear of the hills, because the deep galleries kept breaking into older workings that no man had cut, smooth and square, which the miners walled up and did not enter. In 4A 640 the miners' lord, Stenolf of the Korn, opened the great galleries the North calls the Delvings and was crowned king of the ore hills at Gilvian, and the crown has been bound to the galleries since. Its defining night came in 4A 1567, when the deepest gallery fell in on two hundred miners: the king went down to the rescue himself with a pick and did not come up, and when the gallery was cleared the miners found his body under the fall and his crown hung on the haft of his pick, where he had hung it to work. From the crown on the pick come Mina's laws: every king works a season in the galleries before he is crowned and one every year after; a king's crown hangs on a pick at his coronation before it is set on his head; no gallery is opened into the old square workings, which the miners still wall up; and the mining crown takes pride that its kings dig. Whether the square workings were cut by dwarves, and where they lead, the miners do not ask, and the dwarves of the High Mountains, when they are asked, say nothing at all.

sign.device: A miner's iron pick standing upright with a gold circlet hung on its haft, on slate grey.
sign.origin: The pick is the one the king of Mina took down into the fallen gallery in 4A 1567 and was found under the fall with his crown hung on its haft. It hangs in the hall at Gilvian with that crown still on it, every king since has been crowned by lifting his circlet off its haft, and the miners paint the crowned pick on the gallery doors so that each crew knows its king has worked there.
sign.meaning: Our kings dig. It promises the miners a crown that goes down with them and the strait fleets iron from the North's deepest hills; to the High Crown it says that Mina's king answers to his galleries before he answers to Sonargur.

dynasties.name: The Korn kings of the Delvings
dynasties.notable: Descended from Stenolf, the first king of the ore hills; each heir must work a season in the galleries before taking the crown.

events.name: The Square Workings
events.summary: Leren miners in the Etonia ore hills break into smooth, square workings that no man cut; they wall them up and do not enter, and the custom of walling them holds to 4A 1748.

events.name: The Opening of the Delvings
events.summary: Stenolf of the Korn opened the great galleries and was crowned at Gilvian.

events.name: The Sister Crown
events.summary: The crown of Mine Din was joined to Mina by marriage, and the two ore crowns have had one king since.

events.name: The Gallery Fall
events.summary: The deepest gallery of the Delvings fell in on two hundred miners; the king went down to the rescue himself and did not come up, and every king since has worked his season in the galleries in his memory.

countries.capitalReason: Gilvian lies below the ore hills at the mouth of the Delvings, where the ore comes out of the galleries and the road runs down to the coast.
countries.today: About two hundred thousand people live in the Etonia ore hills with Mine Din, Fargur and Thowson under the mining crown. Mina's iron goes to the strait fleets and to the forges of the North, and its king has worked his season in the galleries.

divergence.what: Mina sells all its iron to the Leren Compact in the last war.
divergence.consequence: The North's forges and fleets are fed from the Delvings, and Mina is counted Sonargur's friend.

divergence.what: Mina sells its iron to Aenor across the strait.
divergence.consequence: The southern crown's armouries are fed from the North's own hills, and Sonargur takes it as betrayal.

countries.name: Dolpar

founding.story: The walled towns of the lake Dolpar, the Hold, Stork, Cinargo and Solenkovi, had traded across their deep lake since the Raiding Years, and their merchants grew tired of riding to Eekedor to settle every quarrel. In 4A 1580 the four towns and the lake market of Parur set up a lake-court of their own and swore to obey it, and the lake league has ruled the lake ring since, a rival in arbitration to the counting houses of the vale.

roots.story: The lake Dolpar is deep, cold and ringed by hills, and its people say it has no bottom, only darker water. In the Raiding Years, when the walled towns of the lake ring, the Hold, Stork, Cinargo and Solenkovi, built the walls that still stand, raiders could take a town by land but none by water, and the towns learned to meet on the lake. When a quarrel arose between them, each town sent one boat to the middle of the lake, where no shore was nearer to one town than another; the four boats were lashed together and the quarrel was judged there by the four steersmen, and the lake people said that a judgement made on the deep water would sink anyone who broke it. This Mid-Lake Moot was the lake ring's only rule for centuries, and when the towns' merchants grew tired of riding to Eekedor's Arbitration Court to settle every quarrel, they made it a court again in 4A 1580: the lake-court of Parur, whose judges still sit afloat on the first day of every session. From the four boats come the league's customs: every town has one voice, as every boat had one oar; a judgement is sworn on the water; no town may build a harbour to rival Parur's, the market all four can reach in a day; and the rivalry with Eekedor, which the lake-court regards as a shop that sells judgements by weight. The Judgement of the Mills in 4A 1694, the first the lake-court gave beyond the lake, was given afloat.

sign.device: A white boat with four oars seen from above, on deep lake blue.
sign.origin: The four-oared boat is the four boats of the Mid-Lake Moot, lashed together in the middle of the lake so that no shore was nearer to one town than another. When the lake-court was founded at Parur in 4A 1580 its judges took their seats afloat on its first day under a banner showing one boat with four oars, one for each walled town, and the league has flown it since.
sign.meaning: Judged on the deep water, and sunk if broken. It promises the lake towns one voice each and every crown of the North a court that is not for sale; to Eekedor it says that the lake has never needed the vale's steelyard.

dynasties.name: The lake-court of Parur
dynasties.notable: Each of the five towns sends a judge to the lake-court, and the judges choose one of themselves to preside for a year; the judge of the Hold presides most often.

events.name: The Walls of the Lake Towns
events.summary: In the Raiding Years the towns of the lake ring built the walls that still stand, and the Hold was the strongest of them.

events.name: The Mid-Lake Moot
events.summary: The walled towns of the lake ring settle their quarrels in the middle of the lake, each sending one boat; the four boats are lashed together and the steersmen judge, and the judgement is sworn on the water.

events.name: The Lake-Court
events.summary: The towns of Dolpar set up their lake-court at Parur as a rival to Eekedor's Arbitration Court.

events.name: The Judgement of the Mills
events.summary: The lake-court judged a quarrel between two hill crowns over the mills of the lake's outflow, and both crowns obeyed, the first time the lake-court's judgement was accepted beyond the lake.

rivalries.nature: Rival courts of arbitration, each claiming the North's quarrels.

countries.capitalReason: Parur, the lake-town, is the market on the lake shore that all four walled towns can reach by boat in a day, chosen so that no one town would hold the court.
countries.today: About two hundred thousand people live in the towns around the lake under the lake-court. Dolpar fishes, trades, judges and competes with Eekedor for the North's quarrels.

divergence.what: The lake-court is asked to judge the toll quarrel instead of Eekedor.
divergence.consequence: The lake league's name rises across the North, and the counting houses take it as an insult.

divergence.what: The lake league joins the Leren Compact.
divergence.consequence: The interior of the island is bound to Sonargur, and Eekedor loses its rival.

countries.name: Mustnom

founding.story: The dwarf goblins of the southern hills have lived in their caves below the Solondor ridge for longer than the Leren remember, trading and stealing on the island's roads, but they became a power of the North in 4A 1497, when the boss of Krakur sent his packmen out on the long road that runs across the whole island and, by Leren ships, beyond. Since then half of Mustnom is always away on the roads, and the bosses at home live on what the packmen bring back.

roots.story: The dwarf goblins of the southern hills are a people of their own, neither dwarves nor goblins, and they do not say where they came from; asked, a Mustnom packman says only that his people came out of the hill when the road called them. They have lived in the caves below the Solondor ridge for longer than the Leren remember, trading and stealing on the island's roads, and their history as they tell it begins with salt. In 4A 1497 the boss of Krakur sent his packmen out on the long road across the whole island, and the first band came back before winter with a single sack of white salt from the far end of the road, a thing the caves had never had; the boss poured a pinch of it at the cave-mouth to thank the road and took the rest for himself, and the Boss's Due was born. From the salt come Mustnom's customs: what a traveller brings home is owed to the cave; the spirits of the road are thanked with a pinch of salt at every crossroads, and the Leren find it on their milestones; half the people are always away on the roads, each carrying a pack-frame that is the packman's whole fortune; the Homecoming before winter is the year's one feast; and the packmen's habit, which has made them valuable to the High Crown since they brought word of a Belonton raid three days ahead of its own riders in 4A 1702, of noticing everything and selling what they notice.

sign.device: A laden pedlar's pack-frame with a white salt-bag tied on top, brown on saffron.
sign.origin: The pack-frame is the one the first band of packmen carried home from the far end of the long road in 4A 1497 with a sack of salt tied on top; it hangs above the boss's seat at Krakur, its salt-bag long empty. Every packman burns the sign of the pack and the salt-bag into his own frame, and northern innkeepers have learned that a frame with the sign belongs to a pedlar of Mustnom, who will pay the boss's due on everything he sells them.
sign.meaning: The road gives and the cave takes. It promises the North goods and news from every road and tells every town that a packman of Mustnom always comes home; the locked doors he finds there are part of the bargain.

dynasties.name: The bosses of the iron seat
dynasties.notable: No king rules the warrens; each cave obeys its boss, who takes the name of his cave when he takes the cave. The boss of Krakur, who gives iron to the smiths, is first among them.

events.name: The Long Road Opened
events.summary: The boss of Krakur sent the first packmen along the long road across the island, the beginning of Mustnom's pedlary.

events.name: The Salt from the Road's End
events.summary: The first band of packmen comes home before winter with a sack of white salt from the far end of the long road; the boss pours a pinch at the cave-mouth to thank the road and keeps the rest.

events.name: The Sirtum Brawl
events.summary: A party of packmen was cheated at the toll-bridge of Sirtum, beat the toll-keepers and ran; Tolhon's prince barred Mustnom from the bridge for twenty years.

events.name: The News of the Landings
events.summary: Mustnom's packmen brought word of a Belonton raid on the coast to Sonargur three days before the High Crown's own riders, and the court has listened to the pedlars since.

countries.capitalReason: Krakur, the iron seat, is the largest warren of the Solondor hills, where the boss gives iron to the smiths and where the packmen bring what they have gathered on the roads.
countries.today: About sixty thousand dwarf goblins live in the southern hills, half of them always on the roads with packs of goods. Northern towns welcome their goods and lock their doors, and nobody in the North hears news faster than a Mustnom packman.

divergence.what: Mustnom's packmen bring warning of landings from the black sea in the last war.
divergence.consequence: The North's coasts learn of the dead's landings faster than any courier could tell them, and the pedlars become the North's eyes.

divergence.what: The packmen rob the royal wagons in a hard winter.
divergence.consequence: The High Crown turns on the southern hills, and the long road closes for a generation.

cities.name: Sonargur
cities.legend: The litany-singers of Sonargur say the Singing Quay was built where the first Leren and Aenoran ships moored side by side, and that a king who sells the strait will hear the quay fall silent.
cities.economy: The strait dues, shipbuilding, the royal fleets and the Singing Quay.

cities.name: Kelur
cities.legend: The folk of Lerendor's North say the old western crown is buried under the hall at Kelur, and that the ice country will rise again the day a king of Sonargur forgets to swear by both crowns.
cities.economy: Herding, furs and the old seat of the northern lords below the Loron highland.

cities.name: Viktara
cities.legend: The counting houses of Viktara say that a debt written in their books cannot drown, burn or die, and that the books are older than the town.
cities.economy: Grain of the vale, the counting houses, loans and the Arbitration Court.

cities.name: Farnardur
cities.legend: The cape folk say that the forts of Farnardur have never been taken, and that the Necromancer's hosts broke on them twice because the first prince buried a strait-whale's jaw under the gate.
cities.economy: The strait forts, Aenoran trade and the harbour of the Sea of R'en.

cities.name: Altovian
cities.legend: The marchers say the first margrave walked the fortress line every night of his life and that his lantern can still be seen on the walls in a hard winter.
cities.economy: The fortress line, the march's garrison and the road to Knorvik.

cities.name: Agtosai
cities.legend: The vale folk say the first king of Tolvael was crowned with a circlet of pine-tar and iron from the hill of Kerhil, and that the vale will be free as long as the circlet holds.
cities.economy: Timber, pine tar and iron of the long vale.

cities.name: Gilvian
cities.legend: Miners of Gilvian say the king who did not come up from the fallen gallery still walks the Delvings with a lamp, and that miners who see it go home for the day.
cities.economy: The iron of the Delvings and the forges of the ore hills.

cities.name: Pand
cities.legend: The hill folk say the stone on which the three kings and the dwarf lord swore the Hill Pact still stands in the council hall, and that a king who breaks the pact will not be able to lift his hand from it.
cities.economy: The hill council, hill ponies, peat and wool.

cities.name: Ilmahrim
cities.legend: Men at the High Gate say the white hall is so deep that its dwarves have never seen the snow above it, and that they keep a bowl of snow at the gate for every lord who is crowned.
cities.economy: Iron, gold, gems and bombards sold at the High Gate.

cities.name: Parur
cities.legend: The lake folk say Dolpar has no bottom, and that the lake-court's judgements are dropped into it so that nobody can appeal them.
cities.economy: The lake market, fishing and the lake-court.

cities.name: Migur
cities.legend: The fishers of Migur say the herring of the Onp came back only because the first prince's grandson threw his summer nets into the sea, and that they will leave again the day the ban is broken.
cities.economy: Herring of the Onp, the Sirtum bridge tolls and the isles' trade.

cities.name: Nuadoso
cities.legend: The folk of the double crown say that Nuadoso was rebuilt after the burning with one stone from each old hall in every wall, so that neither crown could ever claim it alone.
cities.economy: Coast trade, fishing and the pass of Belg.

cities.name: Krakur
cities.legend: Packmen of Mustnom say the boss of Krakur can tell by weighing a pack whether its packman has stolen from it, and that no packman has ever fooled him twice.
cities.economy: The warrens' smithies and the goods the packmen bring back from the long road.

lawsAndCustoms.name: The Speakers' Hall
lawsAndCustoms.summary: The shipowners and landholders of both crowns of the High Crown approve its taxes in the Speakers' Hall, and a king who raises the strait dues without them is asked to explain himself to the lords of Lerendor's North.

lawsAndCustoms.name: Crown-sharing marriages
lawsAndCustoms.summary: Neighbouring crowns of the North join by marriages that set both crowns on the heirs; such marriages are settled by the Arbitration Court so that neither side can later call them conquest.

lawsAndCustoms.name: The Arbitration Court
lawsAndCustoms.summary: Since 4A 906 the crowns of the North may bring their feuds to Eekedor's court for a fee and swear to obey its judgement; the lake-court of Dolpar has offered the same since 4A 1580.

lawsAndCustoms.name: The Hill Pact
lawsAndCustoms.summary: Since 3A 806 the dwarves of the High Mountains are bound to come down to any hill crown of Heodwa that is attacked, and the hill council is bound to keep the High Gate's roads open.

lawsAndCustoms.name: The Strait Litany's peace of the whale
lawsAndCustoms.summary: The strait-whale that winters in the Leren water opens the Ship-Blessing when it comes, and the Litany forbids killing one inside the strait.
